source_text: ἐμοὶ μὲν οὖν ἐνθάδε παυέσθω ὁ λόγος, θρασυνόμενος μὲν ἐφ᾽ οὗ ἥκιστα ἐχρῆν· εὐγνωμόνως δὲ καὶ εὐχαριστήσας πῃ, οἶμαι, κατὰ δύναμιν τὴν ἡμετέραν, ἄξιον μὲν οὐδὲν λεγόντων, οὐ μὴν σιωπησάντων παντελῶς· καὶ ἔτι καὶ ἀποκλαυσάμενος, οἷα οἱ ἀποδημοῦντες τῶν φίλων εἰώθασι. μειρακιῶδες μηδὲ θωπείας ἐχόμενον οὐδέν, οὐδὲ ἀρχαιότερον, ἢ περιεργότερον, οὐκ οἶδα. πρόσεστι μέντοι αὐτῷ, καὶ τὸ μὴ πεπλασμένον, τοῦτο σαφῶς γινώσκω· ἀληθὲς δὲ πάντη, γνώμῃ ὑγιεῖ, καὶ προαιρέσει εἰλικρινεῖ καὶ ὁλοκλήρῳ.
thought_title: Ending the speech: thanks spoken plainly
orientation: Gregory ends his speech, sure that its thanks, though unworthy, are sincere.
pass_a_gloss: For me, then, let the speech stop here, being bold on that for which it least ought; yet gratefully also having given thanks somehow, I think, according to our power, [we] saying nothing worthy, yet not having been silent altogether; and further also having wept away, as those of friends going abroad are accustomed. Youthful [μηδὲ or μὲν ἢ] holding of flattery nothing, nor more antique or more elaborate, I do not know. There is present to it, however, also the not-fabricated, this I clearly know; but true altogether, with a sound judgement, and a pure and whole choice.

pass_b_english: So let my speech end here. It has been bold where it least ought to have been; but it has given thanks in some fashion, I think, with a grateful mind and as far as we are able. We have said nothing worthy, yet we have not been wholly silent. It has also wept its farewell, as those who part from their friends usually do. Whether it has nothing boyish or flattering in it, nothing old-fashioned or overdone, I cannot say. But this I know clearly: it has this much, that it is not made up. It is true in every way, from a sound mind and from a purpose that is sincere and whole.
notes: No Scripture. Doubtful reading: the word after μειρακιῶδες is a compendium read as μηδὲ; μὲν ἢ is possible. Either way the clause ends with 'οὐκ οἶδα' (I do not know), so the English puts it as an open question, 'Whether it has nothing boyish or flattering in it, nothing old-fashioned or overworked, I cannot say', which fits both readings and makes no claim either way. The genitive plurals 'λεγόντων ... σιωπησάντων' (as printed) shift from the speech to the speakers ('we'); the English follows that shift. 'ἐφ᾽ οὗ ἥκιστα ἐχρῆν' as printed: 'where it least ought to have been' (bold toward the very teacher before whom boldness was least fitting). 'Wept its farewell' renders ἀποκλαυσάμενος. προαίρεσις is rendered 'purpose' (deliberate choice). 'οἷα οἱ ἀποδημοῦντες τῶν φίλων εἰώθασι' is rendered 'as those who part from their friends usually do' (facing Latin 'sicut qui ab amicis digrediuntur, facere solent'). The facing Latin also reads the doubtful clause as an open question ('An puerile nihil, vel adulatorium; nihilve obsoletum, vel superfluum habeat, nescio'), supporting the English.
